Sam Loyd's Fifteen

InvariantsPermutationsParity
Game: Slide the numbered counters until they are back in order with the empty square in the bottom corner; some arrangements can never be put right.
How to play: Click a counter next to the empty square, or focus the board cursor, move it with the arrow keys and press Enter. Use Shuffle, Cheat, the size buttons and the board menu to try other positions.
4 × 4
Look for the math

A shuffled board looks like a jumble of numbers, but an odd/even test decides whether it can ever be put right. The original page states the test for the classic four-by-four board and then asks what happens on other sizes and on boards that wrap around.

Counting pairs out of order

Read the visible counters row by row, from top to bottom and left to right, leaving the empty square out. Whenever a larger number comes before a smaller one, that pair is an inversion. This port keeps the applet's own numbering, which runs down columns, so even a fresh board has inversions when read in rows — only whether their number is odd or even matters. A starting arrangement is one ordering of the counters, a permutation, and sliding counters changes that ordering.

The odd/even rule that survives slides

Let N be the number of inversions plus the row number of the empty square, counted from the top starting at one. On a four-by-four board, N mod 2 is an invariant: it is the same before and after every slide. A sideways slide does not change either part. A vertical slide moves a counter past three others, so it changes the inversion count by an odd number at the same time as it changes the row number by one: both parities flip and their sum does not. Here only half of all arrangements are solvable. The logic test reaches over 55,000 four-by-four positions and finds no exception.

Why other sizes behave differently

The page asks whether the same rule works for three-by-three and five-by-five boards, and its own discussion says the argument fails there. The test agrees: on an odd-sized board a vertical slide passes an even number of counters, so the inversion count alone keeps its parity while N changes parity. The four-by-four rule is therefore not a rule for every size. A three-by-three search reaches exactly 9!/2 = 181440 arrangements from the starting order, and Cheat reaches the other 181,440; together they are all 362,880 arrangements.

Cheat, wrapping and the two components

Cheat swaps two neighbouring counters and leaves the empty square where it is. Swapping any two counters flips the inversion parity, so a solvable board becomes an unsolvable one that no sequence of slides can repair. On a fresh four-by-four board the applet swaps the counters 8 and 12, not the historic 14 and 15 quoted from the puzzle's early days; both swaps have the same effect. For ordinary boards the puzzle graph is bipartite, with one solvable and one unsolvable component. Cylinder lets a counter wrap vertically in its column, and Moebius wraps it into the reflected column: the page invites us to check that Moebius is always solvable and Cylinder is always solvable when the number of rows is odd. A complete search of all 362,880 three-by-three arrangements confirms both statements for that size; on even boards Cylinder keeps the invariant, while Moebius breaks it at every size tested.

Press Cheat on a fresh board, then press Shuffle several times: the counters move, but they stay in the impossible half. Press Reset to come back.
